facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus lived during the Lower Hettangian to Toarcian stages of the Jurassic period.
facts.quote: fossil_range: Lower Hettangian-Toarcian

facts.statement: The first known fossil of Temnodontosaurus was a complete skull and partial skeleton found by Joseph and Mary Anning in the early 1810s in Dorset, England.
facts.quote: The first known fossil is a specimen consisting of a complete skull and partial skeleton discovered on a cliff by Joseph and Mary Anning around the early 1810s in Dorset, England.

facts.statement: Sir Everard Home analyzed the first Temnodontosaurus specimen between 1814 and 1819, making it the first ichthyosaur to be scientifically described.
facts.quote: The anatomy of this specimen was subsequently analyzed in a series of articles written by Sir Everard Home between 1814 and 1819, making it the very first ichthyosaur to have been scientifically described.

facts.statement: William Conybeare assigned the first Temnodontosaurus specimen to the genus Ichthyosaurus as the species I. platyodon in 1822.
facts.quote: In 1822, the specimen was assigned to the genus Ichthyosaurus by William Conybeare, and more precisely to the species I. platyodon.

facts.statement: Richard Lydekker proposed the new genus Temnodontosaurus in 1889 to separate species with large dental differences from Ichthyosaurus.
facts.quote: Noting the large dental differences with other species of Ichthyosaurus, Richard Lydekker suggested in 1889 moving this species into a separate genus, which he named Temnodontosaurus.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus is generally estimated to be 9 meters long, making it one of the largest known ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: Generally estimated at 9 m long, Temnodontosaurus is one of the largest known ichthyosaurs, although not as imposing as some Triassic forms.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had eye sockets wider than 25 cm, possibly giving it the largest eyes in the animal kingdom, comparable to those of the colossal squid.
facts.quote: Boasting eye sockets measuring more than 25 cm wide, Temnodontosaurus quite possibly had the largest eyes known in the entire animal kingdom, rivaling in size those of the colossal squid.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had a snout longer than its lower jaw equipped with sharp teeth, which inspired its name meaning 'cutting-tooth lizard'.
facts.quote: The snout appears to be longer than the mandible, being equipped with several sharp teeth (hence its name).

facts.statement: Based on numerous complete skeletons, Temnodontosaurus is estimated to have had more than 40 presacral vertebrae.
facts.quote: On the basis of numerous very complete skeletons, it is estimated that the animal had at least more than 40 presacral vertebrae.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus is a basal and the largest representative of the parvipelvian subgroup of ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: Temnodontosaurus is a basal representative of the parvipelvian subgroup of ichthyosaurs, in addition to being its largest representative.

facts.statement: The monotypic family Temnodontosauridae was established in 1974 to include the genus Temnodontosaurus.
facts.quote: A monotypic family, Temnodontosauridae, was even established in 1974 to include the genus.

facts.statement: Phylogenetic analyses and diagnostic problems suggest that Temnodontosaurus is currently a polyphyletic taxon requiring revision.
facts.quote: Various phylogenetic analyses as well as diagnostic problems concerning the genus make it, for the moment, a polyphyletic taxon (unnatural grouping), and therefore in need of revision.

facts.statement: Joseph Anning discovered the first Temnodontosaurus skull around 1810 on the cliffs of Black Ven in Dorset, England.
facts.quote: Around 1810, a certain Joseph Anning discovered the first skull of the taxon on the cliffs of Black Ven, between the town of Lyme Regis and the village of Charmouth, two localities located in the county of Dorset, in the south of England.

facts.statement: Mary Anning discovered the remaining skeleton of the first Temnodontosaurus specimen in 1812.
facts.quote: The remaining skeleton was later discovered by his sister, the now famous Mary Anning, in 1812.

facts.statement: William Bullock sold his collection containing the Temnodontosaurus specimen to the Natural History Museum in London for around £47 in 1819.
facts.quote: In 1819, Bullock's own collection was sold to the Natural History Museum in London for a price of around £47.

facts.statement: Sir Everard Home initially classified the Temnodontosaurus fossil as an intermediate form between salamanders and lizards and named it Proteosaurus in 1819.
facts.quote: In 1819, he thought that the fossil represented an animal that embodied an intermediate form between salamanders and lizards, which led him to erect the genus name Proteosaurus (originally written as Proteo-Saurus).

facts.statement: Henry De la Beche named three species of Ichthyosaurus in 1822, including I. platyodon, based on anatomical differences.
facts.quote: It was in 1822 that De la Beche named three species of Ichthyosaurus on the basis of several anatomical differences distinguishing the specimens, one of them being I. platyodon.

facts.statement: The species name platyodon means 'flat teeth' in Ancient Greek, referring to the distinctive dentition of the species.
facts.quote: The specific name platyodon comes from the Ancient Greek πλατύς (platús, "flat", "broad"), and ὀδούς (odoús, "tooth"), all meaning "flat teeth", in reference to the rather distinctive dentition of this species.

facts.statement: Henry Alleyne Nicholson and Richard Lydekker published a two-volume work on paleontology rules in 1889, which included detailed descriptions of prehistoric vertebrates.
facts.quote: In 1889, Henry Alleyne Nicholson and Richard Lydekker published a two-volume work that served as an introduction to the rules of paleontology for students.

facts.statement: Christopher McGowan moved the species to Temnodontosaurus in 1974, reviving the name originally proposed by Lydekker.
facts.quote: In 1972, Christopher McGowan again used this combination proposed by Hay (although not mentioned), but the latter revised his judgment two years later, in 1974, in which he moved this species to Temnodontosaurus, as originally proposed by Lydekker.

facts.statement: After the original holotype tooth was lost in 1960, Christopher McGowan designated specimen NHMUK PV OR 2003 as the neotype for Temnodontosaurus platyodon.
facts.quote: As the latter has since been noted as lost in 1960, McGowan designated specimen NHMUK PV OR 2003* as the neotype of this taxon.

facts.statement: Mary Anning sold the neotype specimen to Thomas Hawkins, who then sold it to the Natural History Museum in London for £210 in 1834.
facts.quote: After the discovery, she sold the find to Thomas Hawkins, who himself sold the specimen to the Natural History Museum in London in 1834 for a price of £210.

facts.statement: Carl von Theodori described the species T. trigonodon in 1843 based on a colossal specimen found in Holzmaden, Germany.
facts.quote: In 1843, Carl von Theodori described a new species of Ichthyosaurus, I. trigonodon, which he described as "colossal", based on an imposing specimen comprising a complete skull and a partial postcranial skeleton discovered in the town of Holzmaden in the state of Baden-Württemberg, Germany.

facts.statement: The species name trigonodon refers to the visibly triangular shape of the dental crowns.
facts.quote: The specific name comes from Ancient Greek τρίγωνον (trígônon, "triangle") and ὀδούς (odoús, "tooth"), in reference to the dental crown which is visibly triangular in this species.

facts.statement: Michael W. Maisch transferred the species to the genus Temnodontosaurus in 1998, including specimens from Germany and France.
facts.quote: In 1998, Michael W. Maisch moved the species again to the genus Temnodontosaurus, and attributed to this taxon other, mostly very complete, specimens having been discovered in Germany and France.

facts.statement: A 2023 study suggests that the holotype of T. trigonodon differs significantly from other assigned specimens, requiring future re-evaluation of the diagnosis.
facts.quote: However, a 2023 morphological study conducted by Rebecca F. Bennion and colleagues shows that the holotype specimen differs in cranial and dental traits from other specimens since assigned to the species. The authors therefore suggest that a future re-evaluation is necessary for better a diagnosis of T. trigonodon.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani renamed the species T. crassimanus in 2003, distinguishing it from other Temnodontosaurus species.
facts.quote: In 2003, McGowan and Ryosuke Motani suggested that all specimens historically attributed to I. crassimanus appeared sufficiently different from T. platyodon and T. trigonodon to belong to a distinct species of the genus Temnodontosaurus, being renamed T. crassimanus.

facts.statement: Harry Govier Seeley described the species I. zetlandicus in 1880 based on a skull loaned by an Earl of Shetland.
facts.quote: In 1880, Harry Govier Seeley described the species I. zetlandicus on the basis of a well-preserved skull loaned by an Earl of Shetland (hence its name) around an unspecified date to the Sedgwick Museum of Earth Sciences in Cambridge.

facts.statement: Antoine Laboury and colleagues revalidated the species and renamed it T. zetlandicus in 2022.
facts.quote: In 2022, Antoine Laboury and colleagues reestablished the validity of the species by redescribing CAMSM J35176, but moved it to the genus Temnodontosaurus, being renamed T. zetlandicus.

facts.statement: Friedrich von Huene described the species L. nürtingensis in 1931 based on a specimen found in a quarry in Nürtingen, Germany.
facts.quote: In 1931, von Huene described a new species of the genus Leptopterygius, L. nürtingensis, based on a skull and some postcranial remains of a single specimen discovered in a quarry in the town of Nürtingen (hence its name), Baden-Württemberg, Germany.

facts.statement: Maisch and Hungerbühler argued in 1997 that the holotype of L. nürtingensis is well-preserved and should be attributed to Temnodontosaurus.
facts.quote: In 1997, Maisch and Axel Hungerbühler formally criticized McGowan's view, given that the holotype specimen is preserved in an excellent state of conservation and is easily diagnosable. He then redescribed this specimen and considered it to be attributable to Temnodontosaurus.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani classified the species as a nomen dubium in 2003, though later studies maintained its validity and genus assignment.
facts.quote: The species is again considered a nomen dubium by McGowan and Motani in 2003, but its validity as well as its belonging to this genus is maintained in subsequent studies.

facts.statement: Owen attributed a large isolated skull from Lyme Regis to the species I. breviceps in 1881.
facts.quote: In 1881, Owen attributed a large isolated skull discovered at Lyme Regis, cataloged as NHMUK PV R1157, to the newly erected species of the genus Ichthyosaurus, I. breviceps.

facts.statement: McGowan redescribed the Lyme Regis skull as the holotype of the new species T. eurycephalus.
facts.quote: McGowan redescribed this specimen in more detail and made it the holotype of an entirely new species of Temnodontosaurus, T. eurycephalus.

facts.statement: The specific name eurycephalus means "broad head", referring to the taxon's cranial morphology.
facts.quote: The specific name comes from the Ancient Greek ευρύς (eurús, "broad"), and κεφαλή (kephalế, "head"), all meaning "broad head", in reference to the cranial morphology of the taxon.

facts.statement: The Lafarge quarry skeleton was designated the holotype of the new species T. azerguensis in 2012.
facts.quote: it was in 2012 when the fossil, uncatalogued but stored in the Saint-Pierre-la-Palud local mining museum, was officially designated as the holotype of the new species T. azerguensis by Jeremy E. Martin and his colleagues.

facts.statement: The species name azerguensis is derived from the Azergues river near the discovery site.
facts.quote: The specific name comes from the Azergues, a river located near the site of the discovery.

facts.statement: Authors of the 2022 T. zetlandicus study noted that T. azerguensis and T. eurycephalus are too phylogenetically unstable for a monophyletic Temnodontosaurus grouping.
facts.quote: A similar observation is shared in the study describing T. zetlandicus in 2022, with the authors mentioning these two species as too phylogenetically unstable to be included in a monophyletic grouping of Temnodontosaurus.

facts.statement: Richard Owen named the species I. acutirostris in 1840 based on a partial skeleton found near Whitby.
facts.quote: In 1840, Owen named the species I. acutirostris on the basis of a partial skeleton discovered near Whitby, now numbered NHMUK PV OR 14553.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of I. acutirostris was officially found in 2002 after being considered lost for a long time, though parts like the snout are missing.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen was for a long time noted as lost, but this was only in 2002 when it was officially found, although some anatomical parts such as the snout are missing.

facts.statement: Albert Gaudry officially described the species I. burgundiae in 1892 based on a specimen from quarries in Sainte-Colombe, Yonne, France.
facts.quote: In 1892, Albert Gaudry officially described a new species of Ichthyosaurus, I. burgundiae, on the basis of a specimen discovered in the quarries of the town of Sainte-Colombe, in Yonne, France.

facts.statement: The holotype of I. burgundiae was donated to the National Museum of Natural History in Paris on November 12, 1889, and remains exhibited there today.
facts.quote: After the end of the exhibition, the specimen was subsequently donated to the National Museum of Natural History in Paris, joining its collection on November 12, 1889, where it is still exhibited to this day.

facts.statement: McGowan described the species T. risor in 1974 based on three skulls found at Lyme Regis, with NHMUK PV R43971 designated as the holotype.
facts.quote: In 1974, McGowan described an additional species of Temnodontosaurus, T. risor, based on three skulls discovered at Lyme Regis, designating NHMUK PV R43971 as the holotype specimen.

facts.statement: The specific name T. risor is derived from the Latin word Risor, meaning "mocker".
facts.quote: The specific name of this taxon comes from the Latin Risor, meaning "mocker".

facts.statement: A 1995 revision by McGowan revealed that the three specimens originally assigned to T. risor were actually juveniles of T. platyodon.
facts.quote: In 1995, the same author carried out a more in-depth revision of the three specimens attributed to this taxon. He then discovered that the characteristics he had previously judged to be distinctive were in fact stages of growth, the three specimens representing juveniles of T. platyodon.

facts.statement: A life-size concrete sculpture of Temnodontosaurus created by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins between 1852 and 1854 was displayed at Crystal Palace Park in London.
facts.quote: One of the earliest representations of Temnodontosaurus in paleoart is a life-size concrete sculpture created by Benjamin Waterhouse Hawkins between 1852 and 1854, as part of the collection of sculptures of prehistoric animals on display at the Crystal Palace Park in London.

facts.statement: Early reconstructions of Temnodontosaurus recognized features such as smooth, scaleless skin, a tail fin, and large eyes.
facts.quote: These recognized features include smooth, scaleless skin, a fin at the end of the tail, and large eyes.

facts.statement: Early depictions showed Temnodontosaurus crawling in shallow water, reflecting the hypothesis that it came to shore to sleep or breed.
facts.quote: The park's ichthyosaurs are depicted as crawling in shallow water, reflecting the ancient hypothesis that they came to the shores to sleep or to breed.

facts.statement: While the full body color of Temnodontosaurus is unknown, a specimen of T. trigonodon showed dark coloration on its forefins, suggesting some ichthyosaurs were uniformly dark.
facts.quote: Although the full body colour of Temnodontosaurus is unknown, at least some ichthyosaurs may have been uniformly dark-coloured in life, which is evidenced by the discovery of high concentrations of eumelanin pigments in the preserved skin of an early ichthyosaur fossil, and a specimen of T. trigonodon had similarly dark coloration on at least the forefins.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus is one of the largest ichthyosaurs known, though not as large as Triassic giants like Shonisaurus or Ichthyotitan.
facts.quote: Temnodontosaurus is one of the largest ichthyosaurs identified to date, although the species which belong to it are not as imposing as Triassic forms like Shonisaurus, Himalayasaurus, Cymbospondylus or Ichthyotitan.

facts.statement: Specimens of T. platyodon, T. trigonodon, and T. crassimanus are estimated to reach around 9 meters in length.
facts.quote: Based on different specimens, the species T. platyodon, T. trigonodon and T. crassimanus have body sizes estimated to be around 9 m in length.

facts.statement: A possible specimen of T. trigonodon found in January 2021 in Rutland Water is estimated to be slightly over 10 meters long.
facts.quote: The 'Rutland Sea Dragon', a possible specimen of T. trigonodon discovered in January 2021 in the Rutland Water, near Oakham, is estimated to be slightly over 10 m long.

facts.statement: In 1922, von Huene described imposing vertebrae from the Banz Abbey Museum, with the largest measuring 22 cm in height.
facts.quote: In his extensive revision published in 1922, von Huene described a series of very imposing vertebrae from the collections of the Banz Abbey Museum, Germany, the largest of them measuring 22 cm high.

facts.statement: Based on a nearly complete skeleton of T. trigonodon, McGowan estimated the size of von Huene's Banz specimen at 16 meters long.
facts.quote: Based on SMNS 50000, a nearly complete skeleton of T. trigonodon, the author estimated the size of Banz's specimen at 16 m long, as Huene initially suggested.

facts.statement: In 2022, Laboury and colleagues concluded that I. acutirostris should be considered a species inquirenda.
facts.quote: In 2022, Laboury and colleagues share the same conclusions and considers "I." acutirostris as a species inquirenda.

facts.statement: McGowan and Motani followed Maisch in 2003, considering T. burgundiae a junior synonym of T. trigonodon despite osteological differences.
facts.quote: Maisch's opinion is followed by McGowan and Motani in 2003, considering T. burgundiae as a junior synonym of T. trigonodon, despite slight osteological differences.

facts.statement: The synonymy of T. burgundiae is based only on German specimens, as the holotype from Sainte-Colombe has never been re-examined due to its poor condition.
facts.quote: The synonymy is however based only on German specimens, a new examination of the holotype specimen discovered in Sainte-Colombe having never been carried out due to its questionable state of conservation.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus possessed forefins and hindfins that were roughly equal in length, narrow, and elongated.
facts.quote: The forefins and hindfins of Temnodontosaurus were of roughly the same length and were rather narrow and elongated.

facts.statement: Unlike Ichthyosaurus, Temnodontosaurus had an unreduced, three-part pelvic girdle and only three primary digits plus one accessory digit.
facts.quote: Furthermore, the genus differed from ichthyosaurs such as Ichthyosaurus in possessing an unreduced, tripartite pelvic girdle and having only three primary digits with one postaxial accessory digit.

facts.statement: The flippers of Temnodontosaurus displayed strong hyperphalangy, meaning the fingers contained many more bones than in other vertebrates.
facts.quote: Like other ichthyosaurs, the fins exhibited strong hyperphalangy (where the "fingers" consist of many more phalanges than in other vertebrates).

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had fewer than 90 vertebrae, with the vertebral axis and atlas fused to aid in swimming stability.
facts.quote: It had roughly less than 90 vertebrae, and the vertebral axis and atlas were fused together, serving as stabilization during swimming.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest the serrated chondroderms on the flipper may have acted as noise-cancelling structures to help Temnodontosaurus hunt stealthily at night.
facts.quote: These chondroderms likely served as "noise-cancelling" structures, which may have improved Temnodontosaurus ability to perform a stealthy approach while hunting under the cover of darkness.

facts.statement: Preserved pigment evidence shows evenly spaced stripes on the forefin, and the fin tip likely functioned as a flexible winglet.
facts.quote: Preserved eumelanin (pigments responsible for black layer of skin) and "evenly spaced stripes" are also present across the forefin, and the tip of the fin likely acted as a "flexible winglet".

facts.statement: Species of Temnodontosaurus possessed the largest eyes of any known ichthyosaur and the largest eyes of any animal ever measured.
facts.quote: Species of Temnodontosaurus had the largest eyes of any ichthyosaur and of any animal measured.

facts.statement: The scleral rings in the eyes of T. platyodon measured at least 25 centimeters in diameter.
facts.quote: The scleral rings of T. platyodon were at least 25 cm in diameter.

facts.statement: The skull of T. platyodon was about 1.5 meters long, while T. eurycephalus had a shorter snout and deeper skull, possibly aiding in crushing prey.
facts.quote: The skull of T. platyodon measured about 1.5 m long, while T. eurycephalus had a shorter rostrum and a deeper skull compared to other species, perhaps improving its ability to crush prey.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had pointed conical teeth set in continuous grooves in a structure called aulacodonty, rather than in individual sockets.
facts.quote: It also had many pointed conical teeth that were set in continuous grooves, rather than having individual sockets. This form of tooth implantation is known as aulacodonty.

facts.statement: McGowan established the family Temnodontosauridae in 1974, which currently recognizes Temnodontosaurus as its only genus.
facts.quote: In 1974, McGowan established the family Temnodontosauridae, to which it is still the only genus recognized.

facts.statement: A 1999 phylogenetic revision by Motani placed Temnodontosaurus within the Parvipelvia clade of ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: In the first major phylogenetic revision of ichthyosaurs, carried out in 1999 by Motani, Temnodontosaurus is placed in the Parvipelvia clade.

facts.statement: A 2016 revision by Ji and colleagues classified Leptonectidae within the superfamily Temnodontosauroidea, making Temnodontosaurus the sister taxon to Leptonectidae.
facts.quote: In their phylogenetic revision published in 2016, Ji and colleagues classify Leptonectidae within this proposed superfamily, recovering Temnodontosaurus as the latter's sister taxon.

facts.statement: Pending future studies, Temnodontosaurus is currently considered a wastebasket taxon containing large, loosely related neoichthyosaurians from the Lower Jurassic.
facts.quote: Thus, pending future studies, Temnodontosaurus is currently seen as a wastebasket taxon including some large, more or less related neoichthyosaurians dating from the Lower Jurassic.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus utilized a thunniform swimming method, evolving away from the anguilliform (eel-like) swimming of earlier species.
facts.quote: Jurassic and Cretaceous ichthyosaurs, including Temnodontosaurus, had evolved a thunniform method of swimming rather than the anguilliform (undulating or eel-like) methods of earlier species.

facts.statement: As warm-blooded animals with high metabolic rates, ichthyosaurs like Temnodontosaurus were active swimmers.
facts.quote: As homeotherms ("warm-blooded") with high metabolic rates, ichthyosaurs would have been active swimmers.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus likely had great visual capacity due to a high number of photoreceptor cells in its eyes.
facts.quote: The eyes of ichthyosaurs like those of Temnodontosaurus would have a great visual capacity via the high number of photoreceptor cells.

facts.statement: Evidence from stomach contents proves Temnodontosaurus was an apex predator whose diet consisted mainly of molluscs.
facts.quote: This proves that the animal was indeed an apex predator, but its diet consisted mainly of molluscs, with the large number of undigested hooks being compressed into a large gastric mass.

facts.statement: Fossil evidence shows that Temnodontosaurus engaged in aggressive combat, with several specimens bearing healed injuries from other large marine reptiles.
facts.quote: Several specimens exhibit healed traumatic injuries that were likely inflicted by other large marine reptiles.

facts.statement: The size of the teeth that caused the wounds suggests that the jaw tissues of Temnodontosaurus were very thin.
facts.quote: These injuries, combined with the size of the teeth of the animals potentially responsible for them, suggest that the tissues of the mandible of Temnodontosaurus would have been very thin.

facts.statement: A fragmentary Temnodontosaurus specimen was discovered in the Atacama Desert, Chile, in 1988.
facts.quote: a fragmentary specimen was discovered in 1988 in the Atacama Desert, Chile.

facts.statement: The Chilean Temnodontosaurus specimen comes from the La Negra Formation, which dates to the Early Jurassic.
facts.quote: It comes more precisely from the volcanic beds of the La Negra Formation, dating from the Early Jurassic.

facts.statement: Ammonites found with the Chilean specimen suggest the La Negra Formation dates to the Sinemurian stage.
facts.quote: The presence of ammonites potentially belonging to the genera Arnioceras and Paracoronicera indicates that the formation probably dates from the Sinemurian.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus lived between 198 and 185 million years ago (Hettangian to Toarcian) in what is now Europe, specifically England and Germany.
facts.quote: Temnodontosaurus es un género de ictiosaurios del Jurásico Inferior, viviendo entre 198 a 185 millones de años (Hettangiense - Toarciense), en lo que hoy es Europa (Inglaterra y Alemania).

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus species were large animals, reaching up to 12 meters in length, with great muscular strength and were skilled coastal predators.
facts.quote: Las especies de Temnodontosaurus eran animales grandes, alcanzando algunas hasta 12 metros de longitud, de gran fuerza muscular y hábiles depredadores costeros.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus had a body shape suited for catching fast prey: a long snout, a barrel-shaped body, and a tail with two powerful lobes.
facts.quote: Tenía la figura adecuada para atrapar presas rápidas: hocico largo, cuerpo en forma de barril y cola con dos potentes lóbulos.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus eyes could measure 20 centimeters in diameter, making them among the largest of known vertebrates.
facts.quote: Los ojos de Temnodontosaurus podían medir 20 centímetros de diámetro, haciéndolo unos de los mayores entre los vertebrados conocidos.

facts.statement: Despite their impressive size, Temnodontosaurus had blind spots on its head due to the angle at which its eyes were positioned.
facts.quote: A pesar del impresionante tamaño de sus ojos, Temnodontosaurus tenía puntos ciegos sobre su cabeza debido al ángulo en que estaban dispuestos sus ojos.

facts.statement: Temnodontosaurus were large, very resistant swimmers capable of diving to deep zones of Jurassic seas to catch prey.
facts.quote: Eran grandes nadadores muy resistentes y podían descender hasta zonas profundas de los mares jurásicos para capturar sus presas.
